content: Phenylalanine is an α-amino acid with the chemical formula HO2CCH(NH2)CH2C6H5. It is an essential amino acid, meaning it cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be obtained through dietary sources. Due to the hydrophobic nature of its benzyl side chain, phenylalanine is classified as a nonpolar amino acid. The codons that encode L-phenylalanine in genetic material are UUU and UUC. In its pure form, phenylalanine appears as a white, powdery solid. L-phenylalanine is one of the 20 standard amino acids used in protein biosynthesis, as encoded by DNA, and is electrically neutral. Phenylalanine cannot be synthesized by animals and must be acquired through the diet. In plants and most microorganisms, phenylalanine is produced via the shikimate pathway, starting from prephenate. Prephenate undergoes decarboxylation with the loss of a hydroxyl group to form phenylpyruvate. Phenylpyruvate is then transaminated using glutamate as the nitrogen donor, resulting in the formation of phenylalanine and α-ketoglutarate. L-phenylalanine can be metabolized into L-tyrosine, another DNA-encoded amino acid. L-tyrosine is subsequently converted into L-DOPA, which serves as a precursor for the synthesis of dopamine, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and epinephrine (adrenaline). These three compounds are collectively known as catecholamines. Phenylalanine and tryptophan share the same active transport channel to cross the blood-brain barrier. However, excessive phenylalanine can interfere with serotonin production. Additionally, phenylalanine serves as a precursor for lignin, a structural polymer in plants, and is converted into cinnamic acid by the enzyme phenylalanine ammonia-lyase. Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a genetic disorder characterized by the inability to metabolize phenylalanine. Individuals with PKU, known as phenylketonurics, must avoid consuming phenylalanine to prevent its accumulation in the body. This dietary restriction is particularly important for pregnant women with hyperphenylalaninemia, as they cannot properly metabolize phenylalanine. PKU patients must carefully monitor their protein intake, as proteins are broken down into their constituent amino acids, including phenylalanine. Aspartame, an artificial sweetener found in many sugar-free products, is hydrolyzed in the body to release phenylalanine, aspartic acid, and methanol. For this reason, products containing aspartame are labeled with warnings for phenylketonurics, such as Contains phenylalanine in the U.S. and Canada, or Contains a source of phenylalanine in the U.K. These warnings are intended to help individuals with PKU avoid such products. Interestingly, the macaque genome has been sequenced, revealing a natural mutation similar to the one found in humans with PKU. D-phenylalanine (DPA) can be synthesized chemically and is available either as a single enantiomer or as part of a racemic mixture. Unlike L-phenylalanine, D-phenylalanine does not participate in protein biosynthesis, although it can be found in small amounts in aged or processed proteins. The biological roles of D-amino acids, including D-phenylalanine, remain unclear, but some may have pharmacological activity. DL-phenylalanine, a mixture of Dand L-forms, is marketed as a nutritional supplement for its potential analgesic and antidepressant effects. The analgesic activity of DL-phenylalanine may be due to D-phenylalanine's ability to inhibit the degradation of enkephalins by the enzyme carboxypeptidase A. The antidepressant effects may be attributed to L-phenylalanine's role as a precursor in the synthesis of norepinephrine and dopamine, neurotransmitters associated with mood regulation. D-phenylalanine is absorbed in the small intestine, transported to the liver via the portal circulation, and distributed to tissues through systemic circulation. A portion of D-phenylalanine is converted to L-phenylalanine, and it crosses the blood-brain barrier less efficiently than L-phenylalanine. Some of the ingested D-phenylalanine is excreted in the urine. The genetic codon for phenylalanine was the first to be discovered. Marshall W. Nirenberg demonstrated that inserting mRNA composed of repeated uracil bases into E. coli resulted in the production of a protein consisting solely of repeated phenylalanine residues.
